 📐 **Day 16-22 Development Log**

💣 Main challenge: Colouring the land green and the ocean blue.

   This was a mammoth.

🗺️ Approaches:
  * #1 - Direct attack
     	• Had 2 options: 
          - For every coastline polygon, check whether each pixel is inside it. 
            If yes, colour green. After processing all polygons, everything else is blue.
          - For each continental polygon, paint its interior green. 
            Paint the exterior blue except where overwritten by another polygon.    
          Chose Option A as this was apparently simpler.  
	• Tried to paint the whole ocean blue, fill every coastline polygon green, then integrate into plot_all
          - Ocean: ax.add_feature(ccrs.feature.OCEAN, facecolor='lightblue', zorder=0)
          - Continent fill: Tried a simple ax.fill(lons, lats, etc) for feature in reconstructed_coastlines
          - Added ax.set_facecolor("lightblue") & fill_land_polygons() to plot_all().
          - Combined ocean and continent fill into a single function render_landmask()	
	• ValueError: Sequences of multipolygons are not valid arguments.
          - Tried to flatten multipolygons to remove nesting
	• AttributeError: 'ReconstructedFeatureGeometry' object has no attribute 'with_reconstructed_geometry'
          - This means my reconstruction functions do not return Feature objects. They return ReconstructedFeatureGeometry objects
	  - so the flattening (to remove nested multipolygons) must apply on the underlying feature geometry.
            Therefore, extract geometry → flatten → build a new ReconstructedFeatureGeometry with the flattened geometry.
	• AttributeError: 'ReconstructedFeatureGeometry' object has no attribute 'get_time'
          - Tried to flatten multipolygons to remove nesting
	• ImportError: cannot import name 'ReconstructedFeature' from pygplates
	• RuntimeError: This class cannot be instantiated from Python

 ...bottomline: This is a rabbit hole. The deeper I dig, the more the problem spirals. I figured I should switch approach.

  * #2 - Separate concerns: render ocean and land separately 
      [I learned from my mistakes; too much going on in Attempt #1]
     	• Construct a function render_oceanmask(). 
          This was successful. 
          Oceans coloured blue, and continental polygons blue as well since they are not yet filled.
	• Now onto the continents, using a new function render_landmask().
          In the function plot_reconstructed_features(), I already plot coastlines and plate boundaries using ax.plot.
          Question: Why can't I piggyback on a similar logic and use ax.fill each continental polygon in green?
	  Ans: Because those reconstructed coastlines are polylines, not polygons. 
               ax.fill() only works on closed polygonal boundaries. 
               The polylines do not close themselves, define interior/exterior sides, maintain guaranteed winding direction.
	• Tried directly using the pre-made polygons provided in the coastline dataset.
          (did this in tectonics.py, no reconstruction in ui.py! No duplicate reconstruction logic, no split logic chain across modules)
	• Added the functions load_raw_land_polygons(), reconstruct_polygons(time) to tectonics.py,
          debug_plot_polygons() to ui.py to verify polygon loading and reconstruction. Simple plot of coastal outlines.
          [I would like to highlight at this point the application of incremental logic; verifying baby steps like loading
          & reconstructing base polygons, before moving to colour them. This is a marked improvement on Attempt #1.]
	• Now that I have loaded the polygons, I should be able to directly use ax.fill() on them.
	  - Used ax.add_patch(patch), where patch = MplPolygon(xy,closed=True,eetc.) with PlateCarree CRS instead of ax.fill()
            as Cartopy cannot reproject raw vertices via fill.
          
	  It worked! However, on my map, the entire Earth was painted green. The blue oceans were painted over.
	  Thanks to the clean separation of render_oceanmask(), I know my ocean is loading correctly as blue, so the green must 
	  be some kind of leakage or misreading.
	  Maybe the code thinks the ocean is one of the land polygons?
	• Suspected that one of my land polygons isn't actually land, but instead the global shell polygon that wraps the Earth.
          - Tried to add an area filter, a polygon-type filter and a longitude span filter to remove global shell
	  - with the area & longitude span filter, a small patch of ocean was blue but most of the Earth remained green.
          - For the polygon-type filter to work, I needed to call the FeatureTypes. However, 90% of the features were UnclassifiedFeature.
	  - Tried looking at the source dataset again. In particular, examined the meaning of COB (continent-ocean boundary)
            Contrary to prima facie expectations, COB ≠ coastlines. That meant my COB dataset may have contained coastline loops,
            continent polygons, interior holes, ocean-basin shells, multi-polygons, mask polygons.
	  - I also learned that in GPML coastline datasets, land polygons are oriented counterclockwise (CCW), ocean polygons CW.
            Therefore keep polygons whose signed spherical area is positive. Added as a filter to render_landmask().
	  - Finally decided to simply switch datasets, from the COB_polygons_and_coastlines_combined_1000_0_Merdith_etal.gpml
	    to shapes_coastlines_Merdith_et_al.gpmlz.

	    It worked! At 70 Ma...
	    When I played the time animation from 0 to 70 Ma in time steps of 5 Ma, 
	    I realised that the Earth was still coloured green at some snapshots of time... 

  * #3 - Carve out a sandbox to attack only the land-fill issue: green spilling out from continental polygons at specific snapshots
      [I learned from PETRI's transition from Phase I to Phase II: loading, reconstructing & plotting fossil points using the built tectonic layer.
      Better to carve out a sandbox to ensure the fossils are even loading & plotting correctly, before integrating them with the main pipeline.]
     	•  By this point I had some idea what was causing the continents to bleed colour at specified snapshots in time.
	   Suppose at some initial time t, we have a loop connecting a set of vertices. This loop marks the boundary of a continental polygon, X.
	   Now suppose time advances to time t+Δt, so that each point belonging to X is displaced by the according to the transformation applied by 
	   the tectonic model {i.e. If each point i in X has coordinates [p_i(t),q_i(t)], then at time t+Δt they get transformed to [p_i(t+Δt),q_i(t+Δt)]}.

	   It is conceivable that for certain geometries (e.g. a loop with a sharp corner) the displacement of some point j may overshoot that 
	   of another point k, such that the loop connecting those points crosses, creating a self-intersection of the polygon.

	   This has the unfortunate result that the code cannot interpret the "inside" of the polygon, and may instead read the outside 
	   (i.e. the whole Earth) as the "inside". This would cause the Earth to be painted green, when it is really one rogue polygon. 
	   In less severe cases, the entire latitudinal band would be painted green; cartopy's way of restricting the damage.

	   The fact that this only happens with certain geometries, and only at certain reconstruction times, aligns with what the code does:
	   most times, the oceans are blue and continents are green. 
	   At 15, 30, 55 Ma, entire latitude bands are filled green.
	   At 60, 65 & 70 Ma, the whole Earth is painted green.

     	•  Following this train of logic, the easiest solution was to split all such multi-polygons into triangles. 
	   The loops created by self-intersection would simply be coloured green inside. 
	   Hence defined a function 
	   split_if_invalid(shapely_polygon): if the polygon is valid then return it, else 
	   lines = shapely_poly.boundary
	   pieces = list(polygonize(lines))
	   return [p for p in pieces if p.is_valid and p_area > 1.0]
	   
	   and called that function:
	   shp = pygplates_geom_to_shapely(geom)
	   if shp is None: skipped +=1 continue
	   sub_polys = split_if_invalid(shp)

	   then used ax.add_patch() iteratively over the xy coordinates extracted over all subpolys.
	   
	   The problem got better. Not completely gone, but less prevalent. At 70 Ma, the whole Earth still turned green. 
	   But at 55 Ma, where the previous code gave a full green latitude band, now the band is gone. 
	   Shape polygonising solved part of the problem, but there was clearly another source of error. What else could there be?

* #4 - Antimeridian wrap
     	•  The Earth is wrapped at ±180° longitude: [..., 170°, 175°, 179°, 180°, -179°, -175°, -170°,...].
	   Numerically, that is a jump from +180° to -180°, a difference of 360°, even though geographically those two points are adjacent.
	   If a continental polygon crosses that line... in raw coordinates it looks like a monster discontinuity.
	   The plotting library may interpret that as a huge line that goes the long way round the globe.
	   Result: the "inside" of the polygon becomes the outside, and the whole Earth gets filled green.
	   Short version: This arises from feeding a wrapped globe into planar coordinates without unwrapping it first.
	   Proposal:
		1) Detect antimeridian crossing [crosses_antimeridian = (max_lon - min_lon) > 180]
		2) Unwrap, shift negative longitudes into 0-360 space [if crosses_antimeridian: lons = [lon+360 if lon<0 else lon for lon in lons]]
		3) Build Shapely polygon in continuous lat-lon space [poly = ShapelyPolygon(zip(lons, lats))]

     	   At this point the failure became worse. The polygon colour bleed became even more widespread.
	   I suspected I was going down another rabbit hole, thanks to prior experience (hello, Approach #1!)

* #5 - Use Cartopy's ax.add_geometries()
     	•  Instead of letting the tectonic reconstruction engine output correctly split geometries (esp. along antimeridian), 
	   I was splitting them manually after the fact. This explains much of the overcomplication.
	   Rather than this: 
	   pygplates spherical polygon → raw lat/lon list → Shapely → Matplotlib/Cartopy

	   I should be doing this: 
	   pygplates reconstructed geometry → hand directly to Cartopy/Matplotlib as geodetic geometry and let the projection code split it.
	  
	   So the approach became:
	   1) Build a clean geographic Shapely polygon [def geom_to_shapely_polygon(geom): 
							coords = geom.to_lat_lon_list()
							lats, lons = zip(*coords) 
							poly = ShapelyPolygon(zip(lons, lats))
							+ is_valid() + area filters + spherical angle filters]
	   2) Pass it to ax.add_geometries() 
		[for feature in reconstructed: 
			geom = feature.get_reconstructed geometry()
			shp = geom_to_shapely_polygon(geom)
			geoms.append(shp)
		
		ax.add_geometries(geoms,...)]a

	   The Earth was still turning green at 70 Ma, but the oceans were blue and continents green for 60 & 65 Ma.
	   Latitudinal bands of green at 15, 30  and 55 Ma were also fixed.

	   At this point I noticed that at 70 Ma, right as the whole Earth turnd green, 
	   there was a single polygon right on the South Pole that was left blank. 
	   Could this be the problem? This one, rogue polygon?

	   This was a polygon that:
		- encloses the South Pole
		- was valid topologically
		- did not cross the antimeridian in an obvious way
		- but whose winding on the sphere was inverted

	   On a sphere, every closed loop defines two regions: the intended interior & its complement (i.e. the rest of the planet).

	   At 70 Ma, one polygon was being interpreted as: “everything except Antarctica”
	   So when filled, Cartopy does exactly as asked: it paints the whole Earth green, except the Antarctic polygon, which remains white.

	   At this point I realised I was going down another rabbit hole: the landmask polygons are topologically ambiguous on the sphere,
	   and my fixes and filters were massages after the fact. I decided to look into what professional pygplates users do.

	   Hence...

* #6 - Rasterisation
     	•  A raster is a scan pattern in which an area is scanned from side to side in lines, from top to bottom.

	   Previous approaches asked "which side of this polygon is land?" (have to know polygon orientation, whether inside/outside)
	   This approach asks: "For each point on Earth, is it inside any reconstructed land polygon?"

	   Therefore it bypasses the orientation/self-intersection/multi-polygon/antimeridian/polar complement problems.
	   + it is well-defined on the sphere.

     	•  Rather than this:	
		pygplates geometry → convert to lat/lon → force into planar polygon → guess which side is land → fill with Cartopy

	   ...which will always fail at the poles...

	   I should be doing this:
		pygplates geometry → spherical rasterisation (point-in-polygon on sphere) → cache boolean grid → plot with imshow

	   Define a function rasterise_landmask():
		0) Cache landmask (before function)
		1) Load landmask from cache
		2) Define raster grid [lats = np.arange(-90, 90 + resolution_deg, resolution_deg), lons = np.arange(-180, 180 + resolution_deg, resolution_deg)
		  		       landmask = np.zeros(len(lats), len(lons), dtype=bool)
		3) Rasterise "by hand":  [because as far as I can tell, a rasterise function does not exist yet.]
		  i)  Reconstruct land polygons
		  ii) Spherical point in polygon test [for i, lat, in enumerate(lats):
							  for j, lon in enumerate(lons):
								point = pygplates.PointOnSphere()
		
							  for poly in polygons:
								if poly.is_point_in_polygon(point)
								landmask[i,j] = True
								break
		4) Cache [np.savez_compressed(cache_file, mask=landmask, lats, lons)]
		return landmask, lats, lons

	    Then in the function render_landmask(ax, time, resolution_deg=1.0):
		landmask, lats, lons = rasterise_landmask()

		ax.imshow(landmask.astype(float), extent=[-180,180,-90,90], etc...)


	    🌍🌎🌏🌍🌎 AND CONTINENTS GREEEENNNN FOR ALL POINTS IN TIMEEEEEEEEE 🌏🌍🌎🌍🌎 

	    AND SINCE THE OCEANMASK 🌊🌊🌊 IS ALREADY WORKING, BOTH THE LAND AND OCEANS ARE CORRECTLY RENDERINGGGGGG!!!!!

💡 Insights: 
 - "Simple" tasks may have hidden complexity. When encountering future such problems, instead of tackling the problem directly,
   like colouring the land green and ocean blue in the same function at once, it helps to separate tasks and complete one task at a time. 
   One ocean-renderer. One land-renderer.
 - As with early integration of the fossil rotation phase, it helps to carve out a sandbox to isolate only the problematic code (land-rendering).
 - There is no shame in asking how professionals solve problems like land-rendering. Not everything has to be done from scratch.
 - I learned to identify when I am going down a rabbit hole. If patches lead to more patches lead to more patches... it's time to re-evaluate.

   Meta-lesson: Identify the smallest building block of a task that you can do solidly. Do it. Then build up from there.


🧭 Next steps: 
 - Vectorise for more efficiency, as current computation loops over 181° x 361° ~ 64800 points.
 - Merge sandbox code with museum-demo-v0.03 once optimised.
